questions.question: Briefly summarize the paper and its contributions. Do not critique the paper here. The authors should agree with a well-written summary. Typical range: 3-8 sentences.
questions.final_answer: The paper proposes DUBAD, a real-time, online error detection framework for procedural videos that leverages prediction inconsistencies between complementary action detectors (Figure 1, Section 3.1). It ensembles two RNN-based branches with different temporal receptive fields (short s and long l), each containing a robust detector augmented by a Step Attention Module (SAM) that attends to action prototypes (Section 3.2) and a sensitive detector equipped with a Temporal-Aware Dynamic (TAD) module that applies input-dependent affine transforms with a sparsity-inducing loss to amplify sensitivity to errors (Figure 2, Section 3.3–3.4). During inference, a causal mode filter smooths predictions, and errors are flagged via majority voting over mismatches among four prediction pairs to jointly capture execution and procedural errors, including multiple errors within a video (Section 3.5). Trained only on normal videos (one-class setting), DUBAD achieves state-of-the-art online error detection on EgoPER, Assembly-101-O, and EPIC-Tent-O (Table 1), while maintaining real-time throughput (24.4 FPS combined) with 18.8M parameters (Table 2). The paper provides ablations showing the effect of SAM and TAD, the majority-voting threshold, loss components, and temporal ranges s and l (Table 3, Table 5–6, Figure 5–6), and analyses illustrating how sensitive features induce predictive inconsistency on errors (Figure 3–4, Figure 8).

questions.question: Please assign the paper a numerical rating on the following scale to indicate the soundness of the technical claims, experimental and research methodology and on whether the central claims of the paper are adequately supported with evidence: 4 excellent, 3 good, 2 fair, 1 poor.
questions.final_answer:
The methodology is clearly specified and implementable (Section 3.2–3.5; Fig. 1–2), including the SAM/TAD designs and losses (Eq. 1–3), with a causal, online inference and a concrete mismatch-based decision rule (Section 3.5). Empirical support is strong across three datasets with consistent SOTA gains (Table 1), real-time throughput with a lightweight model (Table 2), and comprehensive ablations that justify core design choices: SAM/TAD contributions (Table 3, Table 6), prediction-source selection (Table 4), and the majority-voting threshold (Table 5). Analyses connect the proposed sensitivity mechanism to observable behavior via histograms/heatmaps (Figure 3–4, Figure 8) and demonstrate that robust heads remain accurate for action segmentation (Table 7). Minor concerns include notable per-dataset hyperparameter tuning (Table 12; Figure 5–6, 9–11), modest E-F1 on EPIC-Tent-O despite improved Avg-F1 (Table 1, Table 8), and a small trade-off in high-overlap localization (Table 11). Overall, the central claims—leveraging prediction inconsistency to detect both procedural and execution errors online, at real-time speed—are well supported.

questions.final_answer:
The paper tackles an important and timely problem—real-time, online error detection in procedural videos, including both execution and procedural errors, and supporting multiple errors per video (Section 1; Section 3.5). The main idea of leveraging prediction inconsistency between complementary detectors is novel in this context, and the concrete design—dual temporal branches plus robust/sensitive heads with SAM and TAD—is well realized and empirically justified (Figure 1–2; Section 3.2–3.4). The results are compelling: consistent SOTA across three benchmarks (Table 1) with real-time throughput in a combined setting (24.4 FPS, 18.8M params; Table 2), along with thorough ablations that attribute gains to the proposed components and the decision rule (Table 3–6). 

Limitations include notable per-dataset hyperparameter tuning for temporal ranges and TAD margin (Table 12; Figure 5–6, 9–11), and comparatively modest E-F1 on EPIC-Tent-O despite strong Avg-F1/C-F1 (Table 1, Table 8). Nonetheless, the contributions are original enough and valuable to the NeurIPS community, both methodologically and practically.

questions.question: Please give a substantive assessment of the strengths of the paper. Be specific, avoid generic remarks. This can, for example, include quality, clarity (e.g. well written), or significance, originality (e.g. a new definition or problem formulation, creative combinations of existing ideas, application to a new domain, or removing limitations from prior results.) If you have many, only list the least generic ones.
questions.final_answer:
1. Clear, actionable core idea with novel operationalization. The paper turns “prediction inconsistency” into a concrete online error signal by pairing robust vs. sensitive heads and short- vs. long-term branches, then using a majority vote over four mismatch pairs (Section 3.5; Figure 1). This design directly targets both execution and procedural errors without needing ground-truth task graphs or LLM reasoning.

2. Method originality in sensitivity/robustness shaping. The Step Attention Module (SAM) uses action prototypes to stabilize robust heads (Section 3.2), while the Temporal-Aware Dynamic (TAD) module applies input-dependent affine transforms with a sparsity margin to amplify error sensitivity (Section 3.3; Eq. 3; Figure 2). The complementary roles are well-motivated and distinct.

3. Causal, online pipeline with an explicit decision rule. Training losses and inference steps are fully specified, including cross-entropy and smoothing losses (Eq. 1–2), causal mode filtering, and the mismatch-based voting rule (Section 3.4–3.5). The implementation is reproducible from the main text and figures (Figure 1–2).

4. Strong empirical validation across multiple datasets and error types. DUBAD achieves SOTA on EgoPER, Assembly-101-O, and EPIC-Tent-O (Table 1), covering execution and procedural errors. The gains are consistent across metrics (e.g., F1@10/25/50 on EgoPER; Avg-F1/E-F1/C-F1 on Assembly-101-O and EPIC-Tent-O).

5. Real-time efficiency with a lightweight model. The combined pipeline reaches 24.4 FPS with 18.8M parameters (Table 2), a practical improvement over LLM-based PREGO (1.33 FPS), and competitive despite the ensemble structure.

6. Thorough ablations that pinpoint what matters. The paper isolates the effects of SAM and TAD (Table 3), compares prediction sources for robust/sensitive votes (Table 4), evaluates the voting threshold (Table 5), and dissects loss components (Table 6). These analyses make the contribution attribution unusually clear.

7. Mechanistic evidence that sensitivity drives inconsistency on errors. Histograms (Figure 3) show sensitive heads dispersing probability mass across more classes on errors, and heatmaps (Figure 4; Figure 8) visualize feature sparsity/inconsistency induced by TAD during erroneous segments, connecting modules to behavior.

8. Demonstrated multi-error handling. Unlike prior online approaches that often stop at the first error, the majority-vote design over independent predictors naturally supports multiple and interacting errors within a video (Section 3.5; qualitative Figure 7).

9. One-class training yet robust deployment. Training exclusively on normal videos while attaining high E-F1/C-F1 (Table 1; Table 8) shows that inconsistency-based detection is effective without error supervision, addressing a key data-collection bottleneck.

10. Maintained action recognition quality in the robust heads. The robust detector retains strong temporal action segmentation performance (Table 7), indicating the method does not compromise standard recognition while adding error sensitivity.

11. Sensible temporal design backed by data analysis. The short/long temporal ranges are justified empirically with task-dependent action counts per window (Appendix Figures 12–15) and performance sweeps over s/l (Figure 6; Figure 9), supporting the dual-branch rationale.

12. Practical guidance via hyperparameter studies. The paper provides explicit sensitivity to β and voting thresholds (Figure 5; Table 5) and reports per-dataset optimal s/l/β/m (Table 12), which will help practitioners adapt the method.

questions.question: Please give a substantive assessment of the weaknesses of the paper. Focus on constructive and actionable insights on how the work could improve towards its stated goals. Be specific, avoid generic remarks. For example, if you believe the contribution lacks novelty, provide references and an explanation as evidence; if you believe experiments are insufficient, explain why and exactly what is missing, etc. Unclarities are adressed later, so only list real weaknesses. If you have many, only list the least generic ones.
questions.final_answer:
1. Heavy per-dataset hyperparameter tuning and unclear generalization of the recipe. The method’s effectiveness hinges on carefully chosen temporal ranges (s, l), TAD margin β, and the causal mode filter m, which vary widely across datasets and even tasks (Table 12; Figure 5–6, 9–11). This undermines plug-and-play deployability for real-time assistants. Actionable: (a) report a single default configuration that performs competitively across datasets; (b) add an automatic selection strategy (e.g., validation-driven or momentum-adaptive s, l; β learned per-branch via a constraint or regularizer); (c) include sensitivity curves when deviating from the “optimal” in Table 12 to quantify robustness.

2. Limited evidence on detection latency and responsiveness. The causal mode filter is causal but uses large windows (e.g., m=150 on EPIC-Tent-O; Table 12), which likely introduces seconds of decision lag, contradicting the emphasis on instantaneous feedback. No detection delay metrics are reported. Actionable: report time-to-detect/error onset lag distributions vs. F1 on all datasets; include ablations varying m (Figure 11) together with measured latency, and add a “controlled-delay” setting as suggested in the Conclusion to characterize the accuracy–latency trade-off.

3. Error detection on EPIC-Tent-O remains weak. Despite higher Avg-F1, the error F1 is low (E-F1=27.6% with E-Precision 28.6 and E-Recall 26.7 in Table 8), suggesting limited practical utility for detecting actual mistakes in this dataset. Actionable: analyze failure modes by error type and action duration; evaluate whether tuning s/l toward longer contexts (Figure 6) or adjusting β (Figure 5/10) can improve E-Recall; consider a learned combiner (instead of hard majority vote) that weights the four pairwise inconsistencies adaptively for domains with long actions.

4. Decision rule is hand-crafted and potentially brittle. The “≥3 mismatches” threshold is selected via ablation (Table 5) but remains a hard rule over argmax labels. This discards uncertainty information in the softmax scores that could capture near-misses or partial agreement. Actionable: (a) compare against probabilistic inconsistency measures (e.g., KL/JS divergence between distributions) and calibrated entropy thresholds; (b) evaluate a light meta-classifier over the four logits pairs to learn the decision boundary; (c) consider per-branch confidence calibration to avoid overconfident but wrong sensitive predictions.

5. SAM’s reliance on fixed action prototypes may hinder out-of-distribution robustness. The Step Attention Module (Section 3.2) uses averaged per-class prototypes from normal videos, which presumes a stable action taxonomy and consistent feature semantics. There is no analysis on drift (e.g., different camera/device domains) or unseen/rare actions. Actionable: (a) add cross-domain or cross-task transfer tests (train on a subset of tasks or subjects; test on held-out ones); (b) evaluate prototype robustness to class imbalance; (c) compare to alternatives such as instance-wise memory or online-updated prototypes.

6. TAD objective lacks a clear justification for “sparsity” and selection. The TAD loss (Eq. 3) constrains the norm of Hk but is not an explicit sparsity penalty; the link to feature selection is mostly empirical via heatmaps (Figure 4, Figure 8). Actionable: (a) report quantitative sparsity metrics (e.g., proportion of near-zero channels) vs. β; (b) compare L1 vs. the current margin loss for Hk; (c) ablate the GRU inside TAD (Figure 2) to verify the necessity of temporal conditioning in producing beneficial instability.

7. Missing comparisons to simpler or broader inconsistency/uncertainty baselines. The core claim is that “inconsistency” is an effective error signal, but comparisons are limited to PREGO/DTGL and internal ablations (Table 3–6). Actionable: add baselines using (a) disagreement between only short-vs-long branches without SAM/TAD; (b) stochastic inference disagreement (e.g., dropout perturbations) or small deep ensembles; (c) entropy-based thresholds on a single robust head. This would solidify that the proposed dual-branch robust/sensitive design is necessary.

8. No reporting of variability or statistical significance. All main tables (e.g., Table 1–2) lack variance across runs/seeds. Given the small gaps at higher overlap thresholds (e.g., EgoPER F1@50 is 23.9 vs. 20.9), reproducibility is uncertain. Actionable: report mean±std over multiple seeds; for EgoPER, provide per-task/error-type breakdowns with confidence intervals.

9. Limited quantitative evaluation of multi-error scenarios. Although Figure 7 qualitatively shows multiple errors in EgoPER, there is no event-level scoring that counts how many errors were detected vs. missed, nor fragmentation/merging analysis. Actionable: add a per-error event precision/recall on EgoPER (since Assembly-101-O and EPIC-Tent-O stop at the first error) and report over-segmentation/under-segmentation rates akin to Table 9 but at the event level.

10. Feature extractor dependence and fairness. For EgoPER, features come from TimeSFormer pretrained on Ego4D; for Assembly-101-O/EPIC-Tent-O, features are those used by PREGO (Section 4.1). This mixing may confound fairness and hides the impact of the detector itself across datasets. Actionable: (a) unify the feature backbone across all datasets (at least as an additional controlled comparison); (b) report results with a lighter backbone to demonstrate robustness to feature quality and better reflect wearable-device constraints.

11. Practical deployment claims not validated on target hardware. The Introduction motivates wearable deployment (e.g., HoloLens/Vision Pro), yet runtime is only measured on an RTX A6000 (Table 2). The large smoothing windows (Table 12) also suggest non-trivial latency. Actionable: provide throughput and latency on an edge device or with mobile-class GPUs/CPUs, and include memory/energy profiles.

12. Limited error-type breakdown on EgoPER. The paper asserts coverage of nuanced execution errors (Section 1; Section 3.5), but quantitative breakdown by execution error categories (e.g., addition, modification, slip) is absent; only qualitative examples are shown (Figure 7). Actionable: add per-category metrics on EgoPER to substantiate the claim that subtle execution errors are better captured than prior online methods.

questions.question: Please list and carefully describe any questions and suggestions for the authors. Think of the things where a response from the author can change your opinion, clarify a confusion or address a limitation. This is important for a productive rebuttal and discussion phase with the authors. Do not simply repeat all the weaknesses.
questions.final_answer:
1. Decision rule and mismatch definition
- Section 3.5 and Fig. 1 (middle) mention “four pairs” and “three mismatches,” while the figure text shows “avg max(·)”. Please precisely define a “mismatch”: is it equality of argmax labels after the causal mode filter, or something involving averaged maximum confidences? Are mismatches computed before/after smoothing? Clarify tie handling and whether per-frame or windowed comparisons are used. A precise spec (with pseudocode) would help reproducibility and may affect my confidence in the results.

2. Majority-vote ablation anomaly
- Table 5 reports identical results for “1” and “2” mismatches on both Assembly-101-O and EPIC-Tent-O. Is this a copy/paste error or due to rounding? If correct, why do 1 vs 2 mismatches yield exactly the same metrics? Please verify and, if needed, provide corrected numbers.

3. Detection latency and responsiveness
- The causal mode filter introduces delay (m frames). With m up to 150 on EPIC-Tent-O (Table 12), the latency could be substantial. Could you report time-to-detect (mean/median) from error onset and the accuracy–latency trade-off as m varies (extending Fig. 11 with latency curves)? Also include a no-filter baseline (m=1) to quantify the zero-latency operating point.

4. EPIC-Tent-O error recall
- E-F1 and E-Recall are low on EPIC-Tent-O (Table 1, Table 8). Can you analyze failure modes (e.g., long actions, subtle visual changes) and show whether adjusting temporal ranges (Figure 6) or β (Figure 5/10) improves E-Recall? A per-error-type or per-duration breakdown could clarify whether a simple retuning or an inference tweak (e.g., per-pair weighting) helps.

5. Role and stability of ˆa (auxiliary path)
- Section 3.3 adds an auxiliary prediction ˆa to stabilize training of the sensitive detector. Please ablate removing ˆa from training and report its impact on Table 6 metrics and on the dispersion behavior in Fig. 3. This will clarify whether ˆa is essential to obtain “useful instability” without excessive false positives.

6. TAD loss justification and sparsity quantification
- Eq. (3) uses a hinge on the mean squared norm of Hk and is described as controlling “sparsity.” Could you (a) confirm the denominator “1/(2Dk−1)” (potential typo?) and explain the intended scaling, (b) report actual sparsity measures (e.g., fraction of near-zero channels in H/W/B or ˆX) as β varies (cf. Fig. 5), and (c) compare against L1 or group-sparse penalties to support the chosen form?

7. SAM prototypes and robustness
- Section 3.2 computes fixed class prototypes from training frames and excludes background. Please (a) show sensitivity to class imbalance and sample count per prototype, (b) ablate adding a background/negative prototype or a learnable “background attractor,” and (c) discuss or test online prototype updating to mitigate domain shift. Even a small cross-subject/cross-task split would strengthen the robustness claim.

8. Learned inconsistency vs hard voting
- The current rule (≥3 mismatches) is hand-crafted. Could you add a light learned combiner baseline (e.g., logistic regression on per-pair divergences or confidences) and a probabilistic inconsistency measure (e.g., KL/JS divergence, entropy thresholds) to show that the proposed hard voting is near-optimal? This could help especially on EPIC-Tent-O.

9. Hyperparameter generalization
- The optimal s, l, β, m differ widely across datasets/tasks (Table 12; Fig. 5–6, 9–11). To assess deployability, please (a) report a “single default” configuration that works across all three datasets and its performance delta from tuned settings, and (b) outline or provide a simple automatic selection strategy (e.g., using estimated action duration statistics as in Appendix Figures 12–15) and show its results.

10. Multiple-error quantification
- Section 3.5 and Fig. 7 emphasize multiple errors, but Assembly-101-O/EPIC-Tent-O stop at the first error and EgoPER results are segment-F1. Could you add per-error event precision/recall on EgoPER (counting errors detected vs. missed, split/merge rates) to substantiate multi-error handling quantitatively?

11. Uncertainty and calibration
- Since inconsistencies arise from sensitive heads being more “unstable” (Fig. 3–4, 8), are the heads calibrated? Please report calibration metrics (e.g., ECE) for a_s/a_l vs. ˆb_s/ˆb_l and consider whether temperature scaling improves the decision rule. This could reduce overconfident false positive spikes from sensitive heads.

12. Reproducibility and variance
- Main tables lack variability estimates. Please provide mean±std over multiple seeds for Table 1 and Table 2 and, if feasible, per-task breakdowns on EgoPER to contextualize the F1 gaps (e.g., the modest margin on F1@50). This will increase confidence in robustness of gains.

13. Fairness of feature extractors
- Section 4.1 uses TimeSFormer on EgoPER but PREGO features on Assembly-101-O/EPIC-Tent-O. To isolate the detector’s contribution, can you provide an additional comparison where all methods use the same backbone features on at least one dataset (even if not fully optimized), or show DUBAD’s sensitivity to a lighter backbone more suitable for wearables?

14. Implementation sharing across branches
- Implementation Details note: “modules in Fig. 1 with the same name share the same weight.” Do SAM weights fully share between robust and sensitive detectors across short and long branches? Are any GRU or head weights shared across detectors? Clarify the sharing pattern and whether removing sharing changes Table 3 outcomes.

15. Evaluation mapping details
- For Assembly-101-O/EPIC-Tent-O you downsample frames and flag a segment as error if any frame within is detected (Section 4.1). For EgoPER, could you detail how frame-level detections map to segments for F1@{10,25,50}? A brief algorithmic description would reduce ambiguity for re-implementation.

16. Practical deployment claims
- Table 2 reports GPU throughput on an RTX A6000. Given the wearable-device motivation (Introduction), can you share measurements on an edge/mobile setup (even simulated via TDP-capped GPU) and rough memory/energy footprints? If not possible, please discuss expected bottlenecks and mitigation (e.g., quantization, smaller s/l, prototype caching).
